newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Flexible EU to let some move faster than others.
newsitem.headline: Flexible EU to let some move faster than others.

text.p: Two-tier, multi-speed, hard core, vanguard, enhanced cooperation -- call it what you will, but flexibility is Europe's buzzword.

The accepted premise is that the 15-member bloc needs to do something to shake itself out of its existing decision-making inertia, especially as it embarks on an ambitious eastward expansion that could double the number of member states in the next decade or so.
In short, flexibility would allow some countries to forge ahead of others, adopting specific policies and integrating more closely, without the threat of a veto from an unwilling partner.
The other, more reluctant, partners would be allowed to join in and catch up when they felt ready to do so.

Much of the momentum for incorporating the concept of flexibility into a new European Union treaty to be agreed at a summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday came from frustration with Britain's Euro-sceptic Conservative government.
But even with a more EU-friendly Labour government, the keenest integrationists -- notably Germany and France -- remain unwilling to be held up by the others.

As a matter of general principle, the treaty is expected to say that flexibility would have to be consistent with general EU objectives, would only be used as a last resort, should ideally embrace a majority of member states and should not disadvantage those not taking part.
In practical terms, flexibility is most likely in areas of immigration, security and crime-busting.

The Schengen Agreement, allowing for border-free movement between most EU states, but from which Britain and Ireland want an opt-out because of their island status, is one area where flexibility has been adopted.
Certain subjects -- such as the single market, major common policies like agriculture and commercial policy -- are clearly no-go areas for flexibility.

Several members, notably Britain and the Nordics, have warned, however, that an over-ambitious hard-core approach could risk being divisive and ultimately lead to disintegration rather than closer integration.
Another area of possible dispute in the last minute treaty negotiations is how one group of countries can decide to move ahead.
Those keenest on integration favour a majority vote. The others say member countries should not be allowed to move ahead without the agreement of all.
